strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenge of unknown/evolving objective weights in multi-objective LLM alignment
Sound theoretical framework with rigorous game-theoretic formulation and proofs showing reduction to convex optimization
Practical algorithm design bridging theory and implementation with efficient blockwise variants and minimal computational overhead
Comprehensive experiments across three datasets with consistent improvements (57-70% win rates) and informative ablations on key hyperparameters
Clear presentation with good intuitions and detailed analysis of weight/value dynamics during decoding
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty—applies standard minimax theorem and Nash equilibrium techniques to new problem domain without fundamental algorithmic contributions
Value function approximation (Eq. 9) is poorly analyzed: assumes final reward is good proxy for intermediate expected rewards, with no robustness analysis or experiments on V_g quality degradation
Weak baseline comparisons: UNIFORM is easily defeated, MOD surprisingly underperforms UNIFORM (suggests implementation issues), hardcoded weights not optimally tuned

Incomplete analysis of failure modes and fundamental limitations: ValuePrism degradation at 10+ objectives underexplored; no investigation of incompatible objectives; worst-case optimization's pessimism not discussed
Hyperparameter λ requires dataset-specific tuning (Figure 3c) with no principled selection method, contradicting the 'no information needed' claim
Missing human evaluation of alignment quality despite claiming to improve balanced alignment; no validation that worst-case rewards correlate with user satisfaction
Approximation error analysis lacking: K-sample approximation (Eq. 10) convergence unanalyzed; argmax sampling bias (Sec. 4.3) not quantified
Scalability concerns: performance degrades noticeably with 10 objectives (Fig. 6); memory/compute scale with objectives; no exploration beyond 10 objectives
Reward model dependency under-explored: no experiments with biased/noisy reward signals despite acknowledged dependence on reward quality
Implementation details incomplete: value function architecture, learning rates, iteration counts for Equation (12) not fully specified; code URL missing

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses practical challenge of multi-objective LLM alignment without predefined weights
Sound theoretical framework: clean maximin game formulation with correct minimax theorem application and analytical solutions via convex optimization
Computational efficiency: Algorithm 2 demonstrates competitive latency compared to baselines with no statistically significant overhead
Comprehensive ablation studies: tests impact of block size B and regularization parameter λ on performance across datasets
Consistent empirical improvements: 57-70% worst-case win rates over reference policy across three diverse datasets
Clear presentation: well-written with effective figures illustrating the core concepts and weight/value dynamics
weaknesses: Large theory-practice gap: Algorithm 2 introduces three major unvalidated approximations (sampling, direct selection, block-wise generation) with no empirical verification that Nash equilibrium guarantees still hold

Value function training underexplored: critical dependency on accurate V_g functions, but trained via crude CD-FUDGE approximation using final rewards; no sensitivity analysis or validation of prediction accuracy

Weak or improperly tuned baselines: MOD and RS significantly underperform UNIFORM (Figure 2) without evidence of hyperparameter tuning; unclear if RMOD gains reflect genuine robustness or baseline weakness
Reward model quality unvalidated: entire approach depends on good reward models, but paper only acknowledges biases without robustness evaluation or analysis of model disagreement
Limited experimental scope: only one small model (gemma-2-2b-it, 2B), no human evaluation, single language/domain; no evidence the method scales to larger models or diverse settings
Performance degrades with more objectives: both RMOD and UNIFORM degrade as objectives increase from 2-10 (Figure 6), limiting applicability to highly diverse alignment scenarios
KKT analysis contradicted by empirics: theory predicts optimal weights equalize expected rewards (Eq. 33), but Figure 5 shows highly unequal rewards with no explanation of discrepancy
Hyperparameter selection without guidance: λ is critical (reduces to UNIFORM at λ=0.1) and block size B significantly affects performance, but no principled selection method provided
Limited novelty: maximin game formulations for multi-objective optimization exist in prior work (Chakraborty et al. 2024, Ramesh et al. 2024); main contribution is application at inference-time
Reproducibility concerns: value function architecture not specified, learning rates unclear, training convergence criteria missing, pre-existing reward model versions unspecified
Suspicious baseline performance: single-objective baselines achieve worst-case reward ≈0.2 (implausibly low), suggesting potential implementation issues or unfair comparison setup

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine practical gap: predefined objective weights are often unknown in real-world LLM deployment scenarios

Solid theoretical foundation with principled game-theoretic formulation and rigorous analysis; correct application of minimax theorem with clean closed-form policy solution (Proposition 3.1) and Nash Equilibrium proof (Proposition 3.2)

Thoughtful practical algorithm design with well-justified approximations (sampling-based expectations, blockwise decoding, gradient descent on log-weights) that achieves computational parity with baselines while adding robustness

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse multi-objective datasets (2, 5, 10 objectives) with strong baselines and thorough ablations demonstrating consistent improvements (57-70% win rates)
Insightful theoretical analysis including KKT-based characterization showing optimal weights equalize expected future rewards across objectives
Good reproducibility: code available, detailed appendices, clear hyperparameter specifications
weaknesses: Value function quality concerns inadequately addressed: the method critically depends on accurate value predictions, but no rigorous analysis of how CD-FUDGE approximation errors propagate; performance degradation with more objectives (Figure 6) may reflect value function quality loss

Theory-practice gap: Algorithm 1 guarantees apply to exact computation, but Algorithm 2 uses sampling approximations and approximate gradient descent; no analysis of how approximations affect Nash equilibrium properties of practical algorithm

Evaluation limitations: no human evaluation (all metrics depend on potentially biased automated reward models); worst-case metric is strict and dominated by single poorly-performing objective; modest improvements over UNIFORM in some settings (5-8% at certain block sizes)

Scalability concerns: clear performance degradation with more objectives (Figure 6); tested only up to 10 objectives; requires training separate value functions for each new objective, limiting applicability

Limited theoretical novelty: maximin/robust optimization for multi-objective settings is established in RL; applying known game-theoretic techniques to LLM alignment is somewhat incremental; claimed novelty of 'first in inference-time' setting is narrow given concurrent work on robust alignment

Hyperparameter sensitivity without principled selection: λ and block size B significantly affect performance; no principled guidance for setting these in new domains; practitioners require empirical tuning

Missing technical details: value function initialization from pretrained models not justified; only 4 responses per prompt for training with no sensitivity analysis; no confidence intervals on reported metrics; incomplete baseline comparisons (RS/MOD use 6 weight combinations vs. RMOD's adaptive approach)

strengths: Well-motivated maximin formulation for robust multi-objective alignment with clear practical motivation
Solid theoretical framework: elegant reduction to convex optimization (Eq. 7), closed-form policy solution, and Nash equilibrium characterization
Practical algorithm design with minimal computational overhead (4.5% latency) through blockwise decoding and efficient weight updates
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets with multiple objectives, dual evaluation metrics (rewards + LLM-as-Judge), thorough ablations, and qualitative analysis
Strong reproducibility: promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, extensive appendix, clear experimental descriptions
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: assumes perfect value functions but trains them with MSE loss; no analysis of how estimation errors affect robustness guarantees or convergence properties

Convergence analysis missing: Algorithm 1 lacks analysis of iteration complexity I, sample approximation quality with K candidates, and error bounds on ŵ*; theory assumes convexity but value functions are non-convex

Severe scalability limitations: performance degrades sharply from 2 to 10 objectives (0.40→0.22, Figure 5) with no explanation or solutions; only tested on gemma-2-2b; no discussion of multi-model scaling

Limited experimental validation: weak baselines (primarily UNIFORM and single-objective CD); minimal comparison with cited related work (Chakraborty 2024b, Ramesh 2024); no validation of value function quality or analysis of when RMOD helps most

Methodological concerns: hyperparameter choices (K=16, B=16) unjustified; learning rate η for gradient descent not discussed; DISTILL-RMOD trains on training distribution creating potential distribution shift; no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters beyond λ

Unclear practical applicability: paper claims no need for objective weights but λ is a design choice controlling robustness level; unclear which objective configurations benefit most; no guidance for practitioners on parameter selection

Presentation issues: Algorithm 1 references h(·) before definition in appendix; forward references to appendix material disrupt flow; overclaimed novelty as 'first' work despite conceptual similarity to Chakraborty et al. (2024b) and Ramesh et al. (2024)

strengths: Sound theoretical framework with clean maximin game formulation that reduces to convex optimization
Practical algorithm design with minimal computational overhead (~4.5%) through block-wise decoding and efficient approximations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with ablations and qualitative analysis
Well-motivated problem: robust multi-objective alignment without requiring prior objective weights
Strong reproducibility: public datasets, promised code, detailed experimental setup
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applying standard maximin optimization to LLM decoding; the 'first at inference-time' claim is narrow given prior robust alignment work (Ramesh et al. 2024; Chakraborty et al. 2024b)

Critical dependency on value function quality is largely unexplored: simple MSE training (Eq. 8) may be inadequate for predicting intermediate-step futures; no error analysis or sensitivity studies provided

Substantial unanalyzed gap between theory and practice: Algorithm 1 makes multiple approximations (finite samples, fixed iterations, direct sampling) without convergence guarantees or approximation quality analysis
Empirical improvements are modest and inconsistent: HH shows ~10-20% gain over UNIFORM (within noise in other datasets); LLM-as-Judge differences small (59.1% vs 57.6%) without significance tests

Severe scalability limitations: performance degrades equally for RMOD and UNIFORM as objectives increase (Figure 5: 0.35→0.25 at 10 objectives), undermining core value proposition for many-objective problems

Incomplete baselines: robust fine-tuning (MAXMIN-GRPO) underutilized; best-of-K baselines are strawmen (no value function approximation); no direct comparison with cited prior work on robust alignment
No principled hyperparameter selection: λ controls weight sparsity but no principled approach for setting it; block size B requires manual tuning
Unclear applicability: paper assumes competing objectives but provides no guidance on when RMOD is preferable to Pareto or uniform weighting; limited discussion of correlated objective scenarios

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a practical gap in multi-objective LLM alignment without requiring pre-specified objective weights
Solid theoretical foundation with rigorous game-theoretic analysis showing Nash equilibrium reduces to convex optimization; Propositions 4.1-4.2 properly characterized
Practical and efficient algorithm with only 4.5% latency overhead compared to baselines, enabling deployment in production systems
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three datasets (HH, UltraFeedback, ValuePrism) with up to 10 objectives, including both automatic metrics and LLM-as-Judge evaluation
Extensive ablations on key hyperparameters (λ, block size B) and thorough analysis of design choices including blockwise decoding efficiency
Strong empirical results: 20% improvement in worst-case win rate on HH dataset; consistent outperformance across datasets in worst-case metrics
Reproducibility well-supported with code availability, public datasets/models, and detailed experimental setup in appendices
Qualitative analysis (Section C.9) demonstrates meaningful response differences with RMOD balancing objectives more effectively than baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (KL-regularized objective, best-response policy) are straightforward applications of existing techniques; main contribution is application to robust multi-objective setting

Critical dependency on value function quality inadequately addressed: value functions trained with simple MSE loss on only 4-16 responses per prompt; no analysis of how approximation errors propagate to final performance

Significant scalability concerns: Figure 5 shows performance degrades from 0.40 (2 objectives) to 0.28 (10 objectives); at 10 objectives improvement over uniform baseline is marginal (~0.02); no proposed solutions

Theoretical gaps: no convergence guarantees for Algorithm 1's weight updates; approximation quality using K finite samples vs exact expectation in Eq. 7 uncharacterized; no error bounds or sample complexity analysis

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: λ controls weight sparsity but no automatic selection strategy; different tasks likely need different values; guidance for choosing B, K, I practically limited

Incomplete evaluation: worst-case win rate metric compares only to reference policy; LLM-as-Judge evaluation limited to gpt-4o and 2 objectives; no human evaluation; missing comparison with constraint-based multi-objective methods

Methodological concerns: direct sampling approximation (selecting max from K candidates) is crude approximation to true policy; value function training treats all prompts equally without importance weighting
Edge cases underexplored: limited analysis of correlated objectives (only C.3), behavior with different reward scales, or robustness to value function quality degradation
